summary: Defines the SIP Replaces header, which logically replaces one existing SIP dialog with a new one. It is a building block for features such as attended transfer and call pickup in multi-party call control.

eli5.summary: It lets one phone call take the place of another, like when a receptionist hands your call to someone else and gets out of the way.

questions: what is the sip replaces header
how does attended transfer work in sip
what is the early-only parameter in sip
subtitle: A SIP header that lets one call take over from another, the building block behind attended transfer and call pickup.

tldr.problem: Features such as attended transfer or call pickup need one participant to be swapped for another in a conversation. Doing that with third-party call control needs a central controller, which is not always wanted.
tldr.mechanism: A new INVITE carries a Replaces header holding the Call-ID, to-tag and from-tag of an existing dialog. The receiving user agent matches that dialog, accepts the new call and shuts the old one down.
tldr.outcome: Replacement works peer to peer, with proxies passing the header through untouched. Because it can disconnect people, the receiver must authenticate and authorize the requester before acting.

today: RFC 3891 is a Proposed Standard, and the metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It still defines the SIP Replaces header.

sections.title: Why Replace a Dialog
sections.content:
RFC 3891 defines the Replaces header for the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP). It is used to logically replace an existing SIP dialog with a new one, and it is meant for multi-party applications and call control.

Swapping one participant for another is already possible with third-party call control (3pcc), but that model needs a central point of control. The Replaces header allows the same call control in a distributed, peer-to-peer way. The RFC lists attended call transfer, retrieve from park, and moving from a locally mixed conference to a two-party call as services it enables, and says the list is not exhaustive.

The design uses a new INVITE rather than implicit matching on the Call-ID. The RFC gives four reasons: an INVITE already has the right semantics for a new call, an explicit header makes the intent obvious, the replacement call can have its own unique Call-ID, and there are no adverse effects if the header is unsupported. The header is often used with the REFER method, but the two may be used independently.
sections.eli5: Imagine you are on a phone call and want to hand it to another phone. Instead of a boss moving calls around, the new phone calls straight in and says which call it is replacing.

sections.title: What the Receiving User Agent Does
sections.content:
When a user agent server (UAS) gets an INVITE with a Replaces header, it tries to match the Call-ID, to-tag and from-tag against one of its confirmed or early dialogs. The to-tag is compared to the local tag and the from-tag to the remote tag.

Several error cases are spelled out:

  • More than one Replaces header, a Replaces header in a request other than INVITE, or a contradictory header: reject with 400 Bad Request.
  • No match, or a match on a dialog not created with an INVITE: reject with 481 Call/Transaction Does Not Exist. A match on several dialogs is treated as no match.
  • A match on a dialog that has already terminated: the UA SHOULD decline with 603 Declined, to avoid a race where it rings for an unwanted replacement.

If the match is an active dialog, the UA MUST verify the requester is authorized to replace it. If authorization succeeds, the UA accepts the new INVITE, hands the user interface and other resources of the old dialog to the new one, and shuts the old one down. If it cannot accept the new INVITE (for example it cannot set up required QoS or keying), it returns an error and MUST leave the matched dialog unchanged.

How the old dialog is shut down depends on its type. A confirmed dialog is ended with a BYE, unless the early-only flag is present, in which case the UA rejects with 486 Busy. An early dialog that the UA itself initiated is ended with a CANCEL. An early dialog that the UA did not initiate gets a 481 and is left unchanged.
sections.eli5: The phone checks its list of calls for the one named in the note. If it finds it and the helper is allowed to take over, it switches the call and hangs up the old one. If anything is wrong, it leaves the old call alone.

sections.title: Sending the Header and Proxy Behavior
sections.content:
A user agent that wants to replace one existing early or confirmed dialog MAY send the target an INVITE with a Replaces header. The user agent client (UAC) copies the Call-ID, to-tag and from-tag of the target dialog into a single Replaces header. If it only wants to replace an early dialog, it MAY add the early-only parameter. A UAC MUST NOT try to replace an early dialog that was not originated by the target of the INVITE.

The mechanism matches exactly one dialog. It cannot match an entire call or follow a chain of proxy forking. For that reason implementations SHOULD address the replacement request only to the SIP Contact URI of the target.

Proxy servers need no new behavior and pass the header through transparently. A proxy that forks on application logic, such as caller screening or time-of-day routing, might send the request to an unrelated set of contacts. The RFC notes the request will then fail.
sections.eli5: The helper writes down exactly which call it wants to replace and sends that note to the person on the other end. The post office in the middle just passes the note along without reading it.

sections.title: Header Syntax and Option Tag
sections.content:
The Replaces header is a request header, defined only for INVITE. It MAY be encrypted end to end, and only one value may appear in a request. It must contain exactly one to-tag and exactly one from-tag, and it MAY contain the early-only flag. For compatibility with dialogs from RFC 2543 user agents, a tag of zero matches both tags of zero and null.

The RFC also defines a new option tag, replaces. User agents that support the header MUST list it in a Supported header. A user agent that wants an explicit failure if the header is not supported MAY put it in a Require header.
sections.eli5: The note has a fixed form: the call's name and two secret tags that prove which call is meant. A special word tells others that this phone understands such notes.

sections.title: Worked Examples
sections.content:
The RFC gives two non-normative call flows. In the first, Alice transfers Bob to a Parking Place and later retrieves him from a different phone by sending an INVITE with Replaces and the dialog information Bob shared with the Parking Place. Alice learns that information out of band, for example by subscribing to the Parking Place or clicking a URI on a web page.

The second example replaces an early dialog at the originator. Alice calls Bob's desk phone, which rings. Bob, in the lab and not yet registered there, uses a software user agent that can see his desk phone's dialog state. It sends Alice an INVITE with Replaces and early-only. Alice's UA answers 200, then CANCELs her original INVITE, and the desk phone replies 487 Request Terminated. Bob is now connected to Alice from the lab.
sections.eli5: In one story, Alice picks up a parked call from a different phone. In the other, Bob hears his desk phone ring while he is away and answers from his laptop instead.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC says this extension significantly changes the relative security of SIP devices. Without it, an eavesdropper who learns the Call-ID, To and From of a dialog cannot easily modify or destroy it when Digest authentication or end-to-end integrity is used. With Replaces, requests can disconnect or replace participants.

An INVITE with Replaces MUST only be accepted if the requester has been authenticated with a standard SIP mechanism (Digest or S/MIME) and is authorized to replace the target dialog. Implementations that support the header SHOULD also implement the Referred-By mechanism.

The RFC names four cases where authorization is reasonable: a party equivalent to the replaced party (such as an executive and assistant sharing an address-of-record), a replacement on behalf of the replaced party, a former participant, and a specifically authorized party. Relying on the former-participant case is called more dangerous, and implementations SHOULD NOT rely on it. Because manipulated dialog information could cause the wrong dialog to be replaced, integrity protection of that information is STRONGLY RECOMMENDED.
sections.eli5: Because this lets someone hang up your call, the phone must make sure the helper really is you, your assistant, or someone you chose. Without that check, strangers could kick people off calls.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content: The RFC registers two items. The first is the SIP header Replaces, which has no short form and is described normatively in section 6.1. The second is the SIP option tag replaces, with the description 'Support for the SIP Replaces header'.
sections.eli5: The new header and the special word that announces support were added to the official lists, so nobody else uses the same names.
